docs.title: How to read the documentation?
docs.text:
Here's how to navigate through this documentation:

  1. Start with understanding how to set up CI/CD for the application by reviewing Setting up CICD.
  2. Learn about database schema management and migrations through Alembic.
  3. Understand how to implement application monitoring by following Observability.
  4. Explore the standardized approach to collecting observability data using OpenTelemetry.
  5. Deploy your application to Kubernetes by following Kubernetes.
  6. Setup reverse proxy using nginx for your application by following Reverse proxy using Nginx.
  7. Setup reverse proxy using traefik for your application by following Reverse proxy using Traefik.
  8. Provision & manage using infrastuction as a code using opentofu IAC.
  9. Additional documentation files are available for more specific topics and features.

docs.title: Commands to load the documentation locally
docs.text:
• Below are the commands that can be used to load the documentation on your machine locally.

  • mkdocs serve -a localhost:8001 - Start the live-reloading docs server.

  • mkdocs build - Build the documentation site.
  • mkdocs -h - Print help message and exit.
  • mkdocs gh-deploy --force - Deploy docs to Github pages

docs.title: To use GitHub Actions for CI/CD, make the following changes
docs.text:
Assuming the repo you are going to set up CI/CD for is in the below structure:

.github
├── dependabot.yml
├── workflows
│    ├── dev-deploy.yml
│    ├── docs.yml
│    └── prod-deploy.yml
├── bot_service
│   ├── dockerfiles
│   │   ├── api.Dockerfile
│   │   └── ui.Dockerfile
│   └── src
│       ├── backend
│       ├── frontend
│       └── logs
├── deploy.sh
├── docker-compose-main.yml
├── docker-compose-prod.yml
├── docker-compose-services.yml
└── README.md
  • Log in to the VM.
  • Run the script setup.sh using sudo chmod +x ./setup.sh && sudo ./setup.sh as sudo/superuser to create a deployment group, user, authorized_keys for SSH, and git config for git access.
  • The repo needs to be cloned using deploy keys initially on the VM with all .env files being created in the respective backend at /fantastic-fiesta/bot_service/src/backend/etc/.env and frontend /fantastic-fiesta/bot_service/src/frontend/etc/.env.
  • Use the new user details,keys which are shown as output to setup deploy keys, github actions etc.

docs.title: GitHub Action Secret Details
docs.text: Secret Name Description HOST_DEV/PROD The IP address of the VM USERNAME_DEV/PROD The deployment user created for SSH access SSH_KEY_DEV/PROD The private SSH key for the deployment user REPO_PATH_DEV/PROD The full path to the repository on the VM

docs.title: Add the following GitHub Action secrets for respective environments
DEV
docs.text:
• HOST_DEV
  • USERNAME_DEV
  • SSH_KEY_DEV
  • REPO_PATH_DEV

docs.title: PROD
docs.text:
• HOST_PROD
  • USERNAME_PROD
  • SSH_KEY_PROD
  • REPO_PATH_PROD

Note: - Similary, if you are setting up a STAGING environment and modifying the workflow files. - The secrets are used in the GitHub Actions workflow files to SSH into the VM and run the deployment script. The secrets should be added in the GitHub repository settings under "Secrets and variables" > "Actions".

docs.title: Some things to be taken care of:
docs.text:
• A .env file with contents from the sample at the root level is required for the common services.
  • The main branch is for the development environment, the prod branch is for the production environment. Any code that is pushed/merged into these branches triggers the respective environment deployment; however, this behavior is configurable.
  • Make sure that ports in the health check job for GitHub Actions are updated to get accurate health status upon deployment.
  • Update the Docker and Docker Compose files as needed in the main and prod versions ( i.e, docker-compose-main.yml & ), and add any common service in docker-compose-services.yml as per need.
  • Any files that need not be version controlled should be added to .gitignore like .env, credentials, etc.

docs.title: 2.Alembic
docs.text:
Alembic is a lightweight database migration tool for usage with the SQLAlchemy Database Toolkit for Python.

Read more here.

  • Make sure that SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_MIGRATION_URL is configured properly in the .env file
  • Keep database migration up to date. Navigate to ./bot_service/src/backend and use the command alembic revision --autogenerate -m "Done some foo bar changes in db" to issue a new version whenever existing database models are updated.
  • Use alembic upgrade head before consecutive application starts to keep the database schema up to date.
  • Make sure that every model's base is referenced, for example, for Alembic to be able to detect changes in the existing tables.
  • Use alembic downgrade -1 or alembic downgrade version_hash to downgrade from one version to an older one.
  • Use alembic current to check the current version.

docs.title: 3.Observability
docs.text:
- Collecting necessary metrics and logs from the application becomes necessary when you actually want to know what is going on in your application at a glance.

  • This can be done by, for example:

    • Ingesting logs into one source and querying/analyzing them.
    • Getting numbers for failed/successful API hits.
    • Tracking compute resources like memory/CPU usage over time for unusual spikes.
    • Generating alerts on unusual spikes and much more.

  • This can be done using observability stacks like LGTM, ELK, Datadog, and many more. We will focus on a fully open-source solution like LGTM.

  • LGTM includes using Loki for collecting logs, Grafana for visualization, Prometheus for metrics, Tempo for trace data, and Mimir for long-term storage.
  • Once we have sufficient data, we can build a visualization that looks similar to:

To instrument your application to start collecting metrics, we will use Prometheus.

  • Start Prometheus and Grafana using Docker.
  • Define metrics like counter, gauge, and summary like here.
  • Use the metrics like here to start collecting relevant data.
  • Either expose a /metrics endpoint to expose metrics data or use Pushgateway to push metrics to a source like self-hosted Prometheus, AWS/Azure managed Prometheus by setting a scrape rule which periodically scrapes metrics.
  • Connect Prometheus as a data source in Grafana and use PromQL to start making relevant visuals!

Similarly, we can use Loki and Loki client to ingest log data.

NOTE: While this works, there is a concept called OpenTelemetry which is tremendously helpful since different providers may have different ways of collecting logs, metrics, and traces. This standard helps in aligning that process.

docs.title: 4.OpenTelemetery
docs.text:
OpenTelemetry is a collection of APIs, SDKs, and tools. Use it to instrument, generate, collect, and export telemetry data (metrics, logs, and traces) to help you analyze your software’s performance and behavior.

Using OpenTelemetry makes collecting logs, metrics, and traces a breeze.

  • Configure OpenTelemetry settings and define receiver, exporter, and connector like here.
  • Start the OpenTelemetry collector using Docker.
  • Configure logger for OpenTelemetry to send log data into the collector, which finally exports it to the respective destination.
  • Comment out logger_provider.shutdown() to turn on the OpenTelemetry log ingestion.

docs.title: 5.Kubernetes
docs.text:
Kubernetes is a portable, extensible, open source platform for managing containerized workloads and services, that facilitates both declarative configuration and automation. It has a large, rapidly growing ecosystem. Kubernetes services, support, and tools are widely available.

  • Get the basics and terminology right
  • Understand why, how & when to use various constructs
  • What & how to leverage HPA Horizontal Pod Autoscaler for automatic scaling of pods
  • What are ingress controllers and how to use them for load balancing and routing traffic to your services
  • Use minikube to get start experimenting or directly on cluster from your cloud provider.

docs.title: To get started with deployment on k8
docs.text:
• Understand your application's infra needs architecture
    • Build the necessary images which needs deployment
    • Tag them with respective version and container registry
    • Install Helm and kubectl
    • Once pushed, define helm chart templates for different services and login to your cluster & finally use helm commands to setup deployment, horizantal pod scaler, ingress load balancer & config maps to automatically scrape metrics from the service in the respective namespace etc, setup ingress controllers, refer ingress controller for additional information.
    • All these commands are put together in Makefile to reuse

NOTE: The repo currently contains examples for commands in AZURE. Stay tuned for AWS & more.

docs.title: Setting up reverse proxy using Nginx
docs.text:
Nginx is a high-performance web server and reverse proxy server that can be used to handle incoming requests and route them to the appropriate backend services. In this section, we will set up Nginx as a reverse proxy for our application.

This will allow us to expose our application to the internet and handle incoming requests efficiently.

  • Log in to the VM.
  • Run the setup script reverseproxy.sh as sudo/superuser using sudo chmod +x ./reverseproxy.sh &&sudo ./reverseproxy.sh to configure Nginx as a reverse proxy for your application.
  • The script will install Nginx, set up the necessary reverse proxy rules to forward requests to your application.
  • The script will also create a self-signed SSL certificate for HTTPS support.
  • You can add more rules to the Nginx configuration file as needed.
  • You can also access your application using the domain name if you have set up a DNS record pointing to your VM's public IP address.

docs.title: Setting up reverse proxy using Traefik
docs.text: Traefik is a leading modern open source reverse proxy and ingress controller that makes deploying services and APIs easy. Traefik integrates with your existing infrastructure components and configures itself automatically and dynamically.

docs.title: Traefik takes care of :
docs.text:
• Auto renewal of SSL certificates: Traefik can automatically renew SSL certificates using Let's Encrypt, ensuring that your services always have valid certificates without manual intervention.
  • Dynamic Configuration: Traefik can automatically discover new services and update its routing rules without requiring a restart. This is particularly useful in dynamic environments like Docker or Kubernetes.
  • Others feature like load balancing, monitoring, and middleware for custom properties and much more.

This will allow us to expose our application to the internet and handle incoming requests efficiently.

docs.title: Getting started with Traefik
docs.text:
• Log in to the VM.
  • Simply start the Traefik container using the following docker compose file:
services:
  traefik:
    image: "traefik:v2.11"
    container_name: "traefik"
    command:
        # Base config
        - "--providers.docker=true"
        - "--providers.docker.exposedbydefault=false"
        - "--api.dashboard=true"
        # Entrypoints
        - "--entrypoints.web.address=:80"
        - "--entrypoints.websecure.address=:443"
        # Logging
        - "--log.level=DEBUG"
        - "--accesslog=true"
        - "--api.insecure=true"
        # Let's Encrypt configuration using DNS challenge
        # Uncomment the below lines to use DNS challenge with Cloudflare
        # - "--certificatesresolvers.letencrypt.acme.dnschallenge=true"
        # - "--certificatesresolvers.letencrypt.acme.dnschallenge.provider=cloudflare"
        # - "--certificatesresolvers.letencrypt.acme.dnschallenge.delaybeforecheck=10"
        # - "--certificatesresolvers.letencrypt.acme.email=rahul@newtuple.com"
        # - "--certificatesresolvers.letencrypt.acme.storage=/certs/acme.json"
        # - "--certificatesresolvers.letencrypt.acme.caServer=https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory"

        #  Let's Encrypt configuration using HTTP challenge
        # Uncomment the below lines to use HTTP challenge
        - "--certificatesresolvers.myresolver.acme.email=traefik.yourdomain.com"
        - "--certificatesresolvers.myresolver.acme.storage=/letsencrypt/acme.json"
        - "--certificatesresolvers.myresolver.acme.httpchallenge=true"
        - "--certificatesresolvers.myresolver.acme.httpchallenge.entrypoint=web" # Use HTTP challenge on port 80
    ports:
      - "80:80"
      - "443:443"
      - "8080:8080"
    # environment:
    #   - TZ=Europe/Amsterdam
    #   - CF_DNS_API_TOKEN=${CF_DNS_API_TOKEN} # Uncomment if using Cloudflare DNS challenge
    #   - CF_API_EMAIL=${CF_API_EMAIL} # Uncomment if using Cloudflare DNS challenge
    volumes:
      - "/var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro"
      - ./traefik.yml:/traefik.yml:ro
      - ./certs:/certs
    networks:
      - traefiknet
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: '0.50'
          memory: 512M
    restart: unless-stopped
    ## Additional labels for Traefik
    # labels:
    #   # Enable Traefik for itself (dashboard)
    #   - "traefik.enable=true"
    #   # --- HTTP to HTTPS Redirect ---
    #   # 1. Define the middleware
    #   - "traefik.http.middlewares.https-redirect.redirectscheme.scheme=https"
    #   # 2. Create a router that captures all HTTP traffic
    #   - "traefik.http.routers.http-catchall.rule=hostregexp(`{host:.+}`)"
    #   - "traefik.http.routers.http-catchall.entrypoints=web"
    #   - "traefik.http.routers.http-catchall.middlewares=https-redirect"
    #   # --- Traefik Dashboard Router (HTTPS) ---
    #   - "traefik.http.routers.dashboard.rule=Host(`traefik.yourdomain.com`)"
    #   - "traefik.http.routers.dashboard.service=api@internal"
    #   - "traefik.http.routers.dashboard.entrypoints=websecure" # Use HTTPS entrypoint
    #   - "traefik.http.routers.dashboard.tls=true" # Enable TLS
    #   - "traefik.http.routers.dashboard.tls.certresolver=letencrypt" # Specify Let's Encrypt resolver
    #   # --- Traefik Metrics Router (HTTPS) ---
    #   - "traefik.http.routers.metrics.rule=Host(`traefik.yourdomain.com`) && Path(`/metrics`)"
    #   - "traefik.http.routers.metrics.service=prometheus@internal" # Route to internal prometheus service
    #   - "traefik.http.routers.metrics.entrypoints=websecure" # Use HTTPS entrypoint
    #   - "traefik.http.routers.metrics.tls=true" # Enable TLS
    #   - "traefik.http.routers.metrics.tls.certresolver=letencrypt" # Specify Let's Encrypt resolver

    volumes:
        traefik:

    networks:
        traefiknet:
            name: traefiknet
            driver: bridge

Now any service can managed by treafik by adding the following labels to the service in your docker compose file:

    services:
    # Example service to test Traefik, where you can just add labels to your service
    # and it will be automatically configured by Traefik
    # and will be accessible at http://whoami.yourdomain.com
    whoami:
        image: "traefik/whoami"
        container_name: "simple-service"
        labels:
        - "traefik.enable=true"
        - "traefik.http.routers.whoami.rule=Host(`whoami.yourdomain.com`)"
        - "traefik.http.routers.whoami.entrypoints=websecure" # Use HTTPS entrypoint
        # - "traefik.http.routers.whoami.entrypoints=web" # Use HTTP entrypoint
        - "traefik.http.routers.whoami.middlewares=https-redirect" # Redirect HTTP to HTTPS
        - "traefik.http.routers.whoami.tls=true"
        - "traefik.http.routers.whoami.tls.certresolver=letencrypt"
        - "traefik.http.services.whoami.loadbalancer.server.port=3000"

    networks:
        traefiknet:
            name: traefiknet
            driver: bridge
            external: true
  • The above configuration sets up Traefik to listen on ports 80 and 443 for HTTP and HTTPS traffic, respectively.
  • It also sets up a dashboard for Traefik that can be accessed at http://traefik.yourdomain.com:8080 (make sure to replace yourdomain.com with your actual domain).
  • The whoami service is a simple test service that will respond with its hostname and IP address. You can access it at http://whoami.yourdomain.com. Similarly, you can add your own services to the Traefik configuration by adding labels to the respective service in your Docker Compose file and make sure it's own traefik docker network.
  • The traefik.yml file contains the Traefik configuration, and the certs directory is used to store the Let's Encrypt certificates.
  • The CF_DNS_API_TOKEN environment variable is used for DNS challenge with Cloudflare. Make sure to set it up in your environment and check more providers here.
  • You can add more services to the Traefik configuration by adding labels to the respective service in your Docker Compose file.
  • You can also set up Let's Encrypt for automatic SSL certificate generation and renewal.

  • Add custome headers, properties like file files, rate limiting, authentication using traefik middleware.

  • You can also access your application using the domain name if you have set up a DNS record pointing to your VM's public IP address.

docs.title: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with OpenTofu
docs.text:
Tired of managing your infrastructure manually? Want to automate the process and make it more efficient and spin the infra for different environment for DEV, STAGING, PROD etc with one command ? Look no further than OpenTofu!

OpenTofu is an open-source alternative to Terraform, a popular Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tool. It allows you to define and manage your infrastructure using code, making it easier to automate and version control your infrastructure changes.

docs.title: To get started with OpenTofu, follow these steps:
Confifure your environment
docs.text:
• Install OpenTofu using brew install opentofu or refer installation instructions for your OS.
  • Create a directory such as opentofu
  • With the help of terraform.tfvars.example create a terraform.tfvars file with your own values. This file contains the variables that will be used in your OpenTofu configuration.
  • Modify the modules as per your needs. The modules are defined in the main.tf file. This file contains the main configuration for your OpenTofu project, including the resources you want to create and their dependencies.

docs.title: Initialize and run OpenTofu
docs.text:
• Initialize the OpenTofu project using tofu init. This command will download the necessary provider plugins and set up the backend for your project.
  • Validate the configuration using tofu validate. This command will check your configuration for any errors or issues.
  • Plan the changes using tofu plan. This command will show you what changes will be made to your infrastructure based on your configuration.
  • Apply the changes using tofu apply. This command will create or update the resources defined in your configuration.
  • Destroy the resources using tofu destroy. This command will remove all the resources created by your OpenTofu project.
  • For more information on how to use OpenTofu, refer to the documentation.
